column1: # topic: Chapter 11: The Rise of Democracy, 1824-1840

column2: Andrew Jackson was a Tennessee lawyer, slaveholder, and hero of New Orleans, called "Old Hickory," who won the presidency, strengthened the office, and led the fights over Indian removal, nullification, and the Bank.

John Quincy Adams was a talented diplomat who won the presidency in the House, but his cold manner and nationalist plans alarmed opponents, and he refused to build a party or remove opponents from office.

Henry Clay, the Speaker who was accused of a "corrupt bargain" after backing Adams, later led the National Republicans and Whigs, backed the Bank's recharter, and promoted the American System and African colonization.
John C. Calhoun moved from postwar nationalism to states' rights, wrote the South Carolina Exposition and Protest as Jackson's vice president, and formulated the theory of nullification.
Martin Van Buren, the son of a New York tavern keeper, was a master party organizer who defended parties as useful, succeeded Jackson, and was blamed for the depression that followed, as "Van Ruin."
Nicholas Biddle was the intelligent but arrogant president of the Second Bank who applied for an early recharter and briefly tightened credit after Jackson removed the deposits.
Roger Taney was the Treasury secretary who agreed to remove federal deposits from the Second Bank and later, as chief justice, wrote the Charles River Bridge decision against implied monopolies.
Daniel Webster answered Robert Hayne in the Senate by calling the Constitution the people's government and endorsing judicial review, rejecting the idea that a state could nullify federal law.
Robert Hayne was the South Carolina senator who outlined the nullification theory in the Senate debate with Daniel Webster.
Denmark Vesey was a literate free Black carpenter in Charleston who, on flimsy evidence obtained by torture, was accused of plotting to seize the city and was hanged with 34 others.
John Ross led the Cherokee policy of accommodation, including a written constitution, but was kept out of the removal treaty talks, and his people were forced west on the Trail of Tears.
Black Hawk was the Sauk and Fox leader who recrossed the Mississippi into Illinois and was crushed, in one of the military resistances to removal.
Osceola led the Seminoles' military resistance in the Florida Everglades, which held out longer than the other removals.
David Walker, in his Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World, denounced colonization as a slaveholders' plot, claimed the country for Black Americans, and urged slaves to use violence.

Paul Cuffe was a Quaker sea captain of West African and Wampanoag descent who took 38 free Black New Englanders to West Africa, an early emigration effort later overshadowed by the American Colonization Society.

William Henry Harrison, the Whig nominee and Tippecanoe hero, was portrayed as a log-cabin, hard-cider man of the people, though he came from an aristocratic Virginia family and lived in a 16-room Ohio mansion.
Franklin Plummer was a Mississippi politician who beat aristocrats by playing the common man, then lost his followers when he himself took up a stylish coach and a uniformed servant.
William McIntosh was a Creek chief of mixed ancestry who signed a land-cession treaty and was murdered by Creeks for it, showing the split over whether to accommodate or resist.
